title: The first adhan
hook: a companion dreams the call to prayer, and Bilal, with the best voice, calls it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Medina charter, and the word ummah. Your line was one city, many peoples. Did you learn a neighbor's name? Day two hundred sixty-one.

There's a mosque now in Medina, mud walls and palm pillars. But there's a problem. Nobody has clocks. People are working in date groves, in the market, at home, and prayer time comes, and half of them miss it. So the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his companions sit down to solve it. How do you call a whole town together, five times a day? Someone suggests lighting a fire. Someone suggests a horn. Someone suggests striking a wooden clapper, the way their neighbors did. Nothing feels right. Then, one night, a man from Medina has a dream. And the answer, when it comes, isn't an instrument at all. It's a human voice. Today: the first adhan.
screen: `NO CLOCKS.` → `A FIRE? A HORN? A CLAPPER?` → `A DREAM.`

segments.voice: The man was Abdullah ibn Zayd. In the hadith, in the collections of Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, he dreams of a man carrying a wooden clapper, and asks to buy it, to call people to prayer. The man in the dream says, shall I show you something better? And he teaches him the words. Allahu akbar, God is greater, four times. I bear witness there is no god but God. I bear witness Muhammad is the messenger of God. Come to prayer. Come to success. God is greater. There is no god but God. In the morning Abdullah runs to the Prophet, who says: it's a true dream. Go and teach the words to Bilal, because his voice carries further than yours. And then Umar comes hurrying in, saying he dreamed the very same thing. Now, Bilal. Bilal ibn Rabah was an Abyssinian, a black African man who had been enslaved in Mecca. When he became Muslim, his master tortured him in the desert heat, with a heavy stone on his chest, to make him give it up. The early biographers say he just kept repeating one word, ahad, ahad, one, one. Abu Bakr bought his freedom. And now, in Medina, the Prophet chooses this man, formerly enslaved, from far away, to stand up and call the whole city to God. It's often said he'd climb onto the highest roof near the mosque at dawn to call. Muslims have called him the first mu'adhdhin ever since. Every adhan you hear anywhere in the world goes back to his voice.
screen: `ABDULLAH IBN ZAYD'S DREAM.` · `THE WORDS OF THE CALL.` · `HIS VOICE CARRIES FURTHER.` · `AHAD, AHAD.` · then, large: `BILAL CALLS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to an adhan. If you can, find a recording now, from any mosque, any country, and just listen, all the way through. If you can't, sit quietly and imagine it: a single voice rising over rooftops before dawn, long notes, the same words for fourteen centuries. Notice how it starts: God is greater. Whatever you were doing, whatever you were worried about. God is greater. Let the sound settle into the quiet after it. The bell holds the time.
The first adhan. The call to prayer, taught in a dream to Abdullah ibn Zayd and first called out by Bilal. Today's word.
Your line: bilal calls. Today, at one of the five prayer times, stop for ten seconds wherever you are, and imagine his voice reaching you. Day two hundred sixty-one.

screen: `DAY 261 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TURNING OF THE QIBLAH.`

howItsDone: The adhan is called before each of the five daily prayers, from mosques around the world, and many Muslims answer by repeating its words quietly as they hear them; Sunni and Shia adhans share most of their words, with some differences.

match.prompt: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

myth: the Prophet dreamed the adhan himself
a companion, Abdullah ibn Zayd, dreamed it, and Umar dreamed it too.
Bilal had been enslaved in Mecca
tortured for his faith, freed by Abu Bakr, and chosen to call the first adhan.
before the adhan, a horn or a clapper was considered
they discussed a fire, a horn and a wooden clapper before the dream.

fork.setup: the words of the call have come in a dream to Abdullah ibn Zayd. who should call them out to the city?
fork.reveal: Bilal: go and teach him the words, the Prophet said, because his voice carries further than yours.

original.note: Arabic: the call, the announcement. the one who calls is the mu'adhdhin.

trapdoor: what you thought: the call to prayer is a song.
what it means: a human voice calling the city: God is greater, come to prayer, come to success, first called by Bilal.
what a scholar hears: Abu Dawud 499 and at-Tirmidhi 189 give Abdullah ibn Zayd's dream; Bukhari 604 has the discussion and the order to Bilal.

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 499; Jami' at-Tirmidhi 189 (Abdullah ibn Zayd's dream; teach it to Bilal)
Sahih al-Bukhari 604 (the discussion of how to call people to prayer)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (via Ibn Hisham): Bilal's torture, 'ahad, ahad', freed by Abu Bakr

notes: Adhan wording given in its Sunni form, summarized; Shia adhan adds 'come to the best of deeds' and other phrases. howItsDone notes differences without detail. Confirm.
The wooden clapper (naqus) is said in the hadith to be used by Christians, the horn by Jews; the script says only 'their neighbors'. Confirm.
Bilal calling from 'the highest roof near the mosque' follows a report in Abu Dawud (a woman of Banu an-Najjar); stated as 'it's often said'. Confirm.
The dream's detail of 'four times' Allahu akbar at the start follows Abu Dawud's version; confirm.
